what_its_for: Atezolizumab is a cancer medicine (immunotherapy) that helps your immune system find and fight certain types of cancer cells. It is used to treat several cancers including bladder cancer, lung cancer, breast cancer, liver cancer, and others. Your doctor chose this medicine because it may help slow or stop your cancer from growing.
how_to_take: Atezolizumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or IV line. A nurse or healthcare provider will give you this medicine at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion takes about 30 to 60 minutes. You may be watched for a period of time after the infusion to make sure you feel okay.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and the type of cancer being treated. The most common doses are 840 mg, 1200 mg, or 1680 mg given every 2, 3, or 4 weeks depending on your treatment plan. Always follow your doctor's schedule exactly. Do not skip or delay doses without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule an infusion appointment, call your doctor or cancer care team right away. They will help you set up a new appointment as soon as possible. Try not to miss scheduled infusions because keeping a regular schedule is important for the medicine to work properly.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home because it is prepared and given to you at a clinic or hospital. The healthcare team will store and prepare it safely. If you are ever given any supplies related to your treatment to take home, store them as directed by your pharmacist or nurse and keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, including herbal products, before starting atezolizumab. Avoid taking corticosteroids (like prednisone) or other medicines that weaken your immune system unless your doctor tells you to, as they may reduce how well this medicine works. Talk to your doctor before getting any vaccines, especially live vaccines (like the nasal flu vaccine). Do not start any new medicines without checking with your doctor or pharmacist first.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience any of the following warning signs, as atezolizumab can cause your immune system to attack healthy organs (these are called immune-related side effects): chest pain, shortness of breath, or new cough; severe diarrhea, bloody stools, or stomach pain; yellowing of skin or eyes (jaundice) or dark urine; severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling skin; muscle weakness, numbness, or tingling in arms or legs; severe headache, confusion, or vision changes; fast or irregular heartbeat; decreased urination or swelling in legs; signs of infection such as fever or chills; or any reaction during or after your infusion such as chills, shaking, dizziness, itching, or trouble breathing. These side effects can become serious very quickly, so it is better to call too soon than to wait.
when_it_works: Every patient responds differently to immunotherapy. Some people notice benefits within a few weeks, while for others it may take several months. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular tests, scans, and lab work to see how the medicine is working. Even if you do not feel different right away, the medicine may still be working inside your body. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use atezolizumab if you are pregnant because it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 5 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 5 months after your last dose. Talk to your doctor about family planning before starting treatment. Older adults: Older patients (65 years and over) can use this medicine, but may need to be monitored more closely for side effects. Children: This medicine is generally not approved for use in children. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver problems, as this may affect how you respond to treatment or how side effects are managed.
